## Angles in a triangle {#triangle}

<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/triangle.html" title="Angles in a triangle"></iframe>

::: notes
Drag any corner. The three angles change, but they always add up to **180°**. Ask: *Can you make one angle very big? What happens to the other two?* Try a right angle (90°).

This is an interactive page in the unit's `embeds/` folder, shown in a frame: `<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/triangle.html"></iframe>`. It uses JSXGraph (free, MIT licence), saved in the course, so it works without the internet.
:::

## Parabolas: move the sliders {#parabola}

<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/parabola.html" title="Parabola in GeoGebra"></iframe>

::: notes
**y = ax² + bx + c.** Move **a**: the parabola gets narrow or wide, and flips when a is negative. Move **c**: it slides up and down. Move **b**: the turning point moves sideways *and* up or down. Ask students to predict before you move a slider.

This one is **GeoGebra**, loaded from geogebra.org (it needs the internet). The commands that make it are in `embeds/parabola.html`: change them to graph anything GeoGebra can.
:::

## Lines: slope and intercept {#lines}

<iframe class="stem-frame" style="height: 520px" data-src="https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/graphing-lines/latest/graphing-lines_en.html" title="PhET Graphing Lines" allowfullscreen></iframe>

[PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder (CC BY 4.0). Needs the internet.]{.stem-link}

::: notes
**PhET Graphing Lines.** Choose *Slope-Intercept*, then change m and b. Ask: *What does m do? What does b do?*

Any PhET simulation can go on a slide like this: on phet.colorado.edu, open a simulation, choose **Embed**, and copy its address into `data-src`.
:::

## Solve it, step by step

::: {.put-in-order first="Start" last="Answer"}
- 3x + 5 = 20 | The equation to solve.
- 3x + 5 − 5 = 20 − 5 | Take 5 from both sides.
- 3x = 15 | Now only the x part is on the left.
- 3x ÷ 3 = 15 ÷ 3 | Divide both sides by 3.
- x = 5 | The answer. Check: 3 × 5 + 5 = 20 ✓
:::

::: notes
**Put it in order** works for any process: the steps of solving an equation, of a proof, of a construction. The reasons (after the `|`) show when every step is in the right place.
:::

## Match the formula

::: {.matching}
- A = πr² | Area of a circle
- C = 2πr | Circumference of a circle
- a² + b² = c² | Pythagoras' theorem
- A = ½ × b × h | Area of a triangle
- y = mx + b | A straight line
- V = l × w × h | Volume of a box
:::

## Prime, even, or both?

::: {.sort layout="venn"}
- **Prime**
  - 3 | 3 has only two factors: 1 and 3. It is odd.
  - 5 | 5 has only two factors: 1 and 5. It is odd.
  - 7 | 7 has only two factors: 1 and 7. It is odd.
  - 11 | 11 has only two factors: 1 and 11. It is odd.
- **Both**
  - 2 | 2 is the only even prime number.
- **Even**
  - 4 | 4 = 2 × 2, so it is not prime.
  - 6 | 6 = 2 × 3, so it is not prime.
  - 10 | 10 = 2 × 5, so it is not prime.
  - 12 | 12 = 3 × 4, so it is not prime.
:::

::: notes
A **Venn diagram** (Sort it with `layout="venn"`). Ask: *Why is 2 the only number in the middle?* Then: *Where would 9 go?* (Outside both circles: a good discussion.)
:::

## Math words

::: {.fill-blanks extra="radius, area"}
The longest side of a right triangle is the [hypotenuse]. The angles in a triangle add up to [180] degrees.

In y = mx + b, the number m is the [slope]. A number with only two factors, 1 and itself, is a [prime] number.
:::

## Mental math

::: {.trivia seconds="8" title="Quick-fire!"}
- 7 × 8 | 56
- 144 ÷ 12 | 12
- 15% of 200 | 30
- 3² + 4² | 25
- The angles of a square, added up | 360°
- Half of 3.5 | 1.75
:::

::: notes
**Quick-fire**: 8 seconds a question. Change `seconds="8"` to make it easier or harder.
:::
